Let \(p=\ell\), and write \(R(x,y,z)\) for the property that \(\{x,y,z\}\in\mathscr H\).

Set
\[
q=\frac{p-1}{2}.
\]

### 1. Determining \(\operatorname{Aut}(\mathscr H)\)

For distinct \(x,y,z\), define
\[
N(x,y,z)=\#\{t\in V:R(x,y,t)\text{ and }R(x,z,t)\}.
\]

If \(x,y,z\) are noncollinear, the two linear forms
\[
t\mapsto \det(y-x,t-x),\qquad t\mapsto \det(z-x,t-x)
\]
are independent. Hence their pair gives a bijection \(V\to\mathbb F_p^2\), and each form is required to be a nonzero square. Therefore
\[
N(x,y,z)=q^2.
\]

If \(x,y,z\) are collinear, write \(z-x=c(y-x)\) with \(c\neq0,1\). Then
\[
\det(z-x,t-x)=c\det(y-x,t-x).
\]
Thus
\[
N(x,y,z)=
\begin{cases}
pq,&\chi(c)=1,\\
0,&\chi(c)=-1.
\end{cases}
\]

Since \(q^2\neq pq\) and \(q^2\neq0\), the triple \(x,y,z\) is noncollinear exactly when \(N(x,y,z)=q^2\). Consequently every automorphism of \(\mathscr H\) preserves collinearity.

A bijection of the affine plane \(\mathbb F_p^2\) preserving collinearity is affine semilinear. Since \(p\) is prime, the only field automorphism of \(\mathbb F_p\) is the identity, so every automorphism has the form
\[
x\longmapsto Ax+b,\qquad A\in\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb F_p),\ b\in V.
\]

Moreover,
\[
\det(A(v-u),A(w-u))
=\det(A)\det(v-u,w-u).
\]
Therefore the affine map preserves \(R\) precisely when \(\chi(\det A)=1\). Hence
\[
\operatorname{Aut}(\mathscr H)
=
V\rtimes K,
\qquad
K=\{A\in\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb F_p):\chi(\det A)=1\}.
\]

### 2. Structure of a regular subgroup

Let \(G\leq \operatorname{Aut}(\mathscr H)\) be regular on \(V\). Since \(|V|=p^2\),
\[
|G|=p^2.
\]

Every element of \(G\) has \(p\)-power order. An affine transformation of \(\mathbb F_p^2\) cannot have order \(p^2\): its linear part has \(p\)-power order at most \(p\), and a nontrivial unipotent affine transformation has order \(p\). Thus \(G\) has exponent \(p\), so \(G\cong C_p\times C_p\).

Let \(T\cong V\) be the translation subgroup, and consider the projection
\[
\pi:G\to K.
\]

The kernel \(G\cap T\) can have size \(1,p,\) or \(p^2\).

#### Case 1: \(|G\cap T|=p^2\)

Then \(G=T\), giving exactly one regular subgroup.

#### Case 2: \(|G\cap T|=1\)

Then \(\pi(G)\) would be a subgroup of order \(p^2\) in \(K\subseteq\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb F_p)\). But
\[
|\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb F_p)|
=(p^2-1)(p^2-p)
=p(p-1)^2(p+1),
\]
whose \(p\)-part is only \(p\). Hence this case is impossible.

#### Case 3: \(|G\cap T|=p\)

Write
\[
G\cap T=T_L
\]
for a line \(L\leq V\). Then \(\pi(G)\) has order \(p\).

Every order-\(p\) subgroup \(P\) of \(\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb F_p)\) is generated by a nontrivial unipotent matrix
\[
A=I+N,\qquad N^2=0.
\]
It has a unique fixed line \(L=\ker N\), and \(P\) acts trivially on \(L\).

For a fixed \(P=\langle A\rangle\), every subgroup \(G\) above \(P\) has the form
\[
G=\langle T_L,(A,b)\rangle.
\]
Replacing \(b\) by \(b+\lambda\) with \(\lambda\in L\) gives the same subgroup, so \(b\) is determined by its coset in \(V/L\).

The resulting group is regular exactly when \(b\notin L\). Indeed, modulo \(L\), the orbit of \(0\) under \((A,b)\) is
\[
0,\ b,\ 2b,\dots,(p-1)b,
\]
which gives all \(p\) nonzero cosets precisely when \(b+L\neq0\).

There are \(p-1\) nonzero cosets in \(V/L\). Thus each order-\(p\) subgroup \(P\) produces \(p-1\) regular subgroups.

Finally, the number of order-\(p\) subgroups \(P\) is \(p+1\), one for each line \(L\) in \(V\). Therefore Case 3 contributes
\[
(p+1)(p-1)=p^2-1
\]
regular subgroups.

Adding the translation subgroup from Case 1 gives
\[
1+(p^2-1)=p^2.
\]

Therefore the number of regular subgroups is
\[
\boxed{\ell^2}.
\]
